newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Soft EMU option grows despite calls for budget cuts.
newsitem.headline: Soft EMU option grows despite calls for budget cuts.

text.p: Senior European policy-makers on Tuesday urged governments to whip their budgets into shape ahead of the euro's introduction in January 1999 but left open how much belt-tightening would actually be needed to join.

Bank of France chief Jean-Claude Trichet, presenting the Bank's annual report in Paris, said it was essential that the French government make further cuts in its 1997 budget, the critical year in which countries will be judged on their qualifications for economic and monetary union (EMU).

"Reducing public deficits is indispensible in 1997 as it is in the medium term," Trichet told a news conference, adding that his report was written before the new Socialist government announced its policy programme last week.
Trichet called for continuing wage restraint and said France's payroll deductions to fund the country's welfare system were too high.
In a separate interview with the Paris daily Le Monde, Trichet said it would be "unthinkable" for certain governments not to take corrective action on the budgets.

Doubts over the ability of countries like France to meet the budgetary demands of EMU have grown in recent weeks due to the new government's emphasis on jobs and growth and solemn pledge not to engage in more austerity measures.

The leftward political lurch in France along with the struggle Germany and others are having in putting their public finances in order have raised expectations of a broad membership in EMU, what many now call the soft euro option.

For EMU to start on time with budget deficits in some of the EU's larger economies above three percent of GDP -- the Maastricht Treaty's target -- a more generous reading of the deficit criterion would have to be applied by EU leaders when they decide on the founding members in the spring of 1998.

Fuelling speculation that such an interpretation would indeed be necessary, EU Monetary Affairs Commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said there were no grounds to expect the EU to apply the treaty's rules rigidly.
"There is no question of rigid application...of the 3.0 percent figure," de Silguy told a group of Italian reporters in Brussels.
He also said there was no reason to fear that France, seen as an indispensible member of EMU, would not be ready to take part in the single currency's launch.

The most vocal advocate of a strict reading of the euro's entry rules has been Germany. But even in a country long seen as a paragon of fiscal virtue, the combined force of the government's poor finances and the political imperatives of EMU have prompted a noticeable re-evaluation.
Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Tuesday that whether a country had fulfiled the deficit goal would depend on a judgment of its overall economic picture.
"For good economic reasons...the Treaty is not about simply reaching numeric values," Krupp said in the text of speech delivered in Kiel, Germany.
Those benefiting the most from the soft-euro scenario are southern European countries like Italy, which is expected to see its budget deficit climb well above the three percent threshold.
The Italian industrialists group, Confindustria, said in a report on Tuesday that Rome's deficit would come in at around 3.4 percent of GDP without any fresh budget savings.
The group, however, said it expected the government, led by Prime Minister Romano Prodi, to introduce further budget cuts this year.
Prodi has said he would resign if Italy failed to become a founding member of EMU.
More confident than Italy and widely seen as a front-runner in the euro race, Spain's central bank governor Luis Angel Rojo voiced optimism over his country's chances of making the EMU grade.

In an address accompanying the Bank's annual report, Rojo said policies orientated toward greater stability of the Spanish economy have "strongly raised the probability that Spain joins European economic and monetary union from the first moment."
